An infant in Wisconsin died of measles, marking the state’s first death linked to the disease in 36 years, the state’s Department of Health Services announced on Thursday.

The Department of Health Services said the child died in southwestern Wisconsin but did not provide a more precise location.

The department said it would not release any additional details to protect the privacy of the family.

The coroner listed the immediate cause of death as measles.

“It is with a heavy heart we are reporting the first death of an infant connected with a measles outbreak in Wisconsin in many years. My heart is broken for the family,” state Department of Health Services Secretary Kirsten Johnson said in a statement.

“Any death of a child is a tragedy and even more so when it is related to a vaccine-preventable disease. Measles can cause serious illness and death, and it is important for all Wisconsinites to evaluate their risk and take steps to protect themselves and their family,” she continued.

Measles can cause life-threatening complications, including pneumonia and swelling of the brain. The department said that while anyone can become seriously ill, children younger than 5, pregnant people and people with weakened immune systems are at increased risk of complications.

Wisconsin has reported 431 measles cases in 13 counties so far this year, reflecting the highest number of cases seen in the state in more than 35 years. Among these cases, nine people required hospitalization for severe symptoms.

State officials urged Wisconsinites to be proactive in preventing illness to protect themselves and their communities, saying the best way to prevent measles is with the measles, mumps, rubella (MMR) vaccine.

The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services previously told FOX News Digital that “Secretary Kennedy and CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz continue to make clear that the MMR vaccine is the most effective way to prevent measles.”

Earlier this week, a child in New York state’s Lewis County died in the first known measles-associated death in the state in more than 30 years.

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said she was “heartbroken” to learn of the child’s death.

“As a mother and grandmother, I cannot imagine what this family is going through. My heart goes out to everyone who knew and loved this child,” Hochul said in a statement.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has reported four measles-associated deaths across the country this year, although state health departments have reported higher figures.

In Pennsylvania, state health officials have confirmed six measles-associated deaths in 2026 and are investigating another reported death that has not yet met the state’s criteria to be classified as measles-associated.
news.content: اطلاعات بیشتری از پوشش ما را در نتایج جستجوی خود مشاهده کنید. یک نوزاد در ویسکانسین بر اثر سرخک درگذشت، که اولین مرگ مرتبط با این بیماری در این ایالت در 36 سال گذشته است، وزارت خدمات بهداشتی ایالتی روز پنجشنبه اعلام کرد. وزارت خدمات بهداشت گفت که کودک در جنوب غربی ویسکانسین درگذشت، اما هیچ جزئیات بیشتری از خانواده ارائه نکرد تا از خانواده محافظت کند. کریستن جانسون، وزیر خدمات بهداشتی ایالتی، در بیانیه‌ای گفت: «با قلب سنگین، اولین مرگ نوزادی را گزارش می‌کنیم که به دلیل شیوع سرخک در ویسکانسین پس از سال‌ها اتفاق افتاده است. قلب من برای خانواده‌اش شکسته است. سرخک می تواند باعث بیماری جدی و مرگ شود، و برای همه ساکنان ویسکانسینی مهم است که خطر خود را ارزیابی کنند و اقداماتی را برای محافظت از خود و خانواده خود انجام دهند.» او ادامه داد. سرخک می تواند باعث عوارض تهدید کننده زندگی، از جمله ذات الریه و تورم مغز شود. این وزارتخانه گفت که در حالی که هر کسی ممکن است به طور جدی بیمار شود، کودکان کمتر از 5 سال، افراد باردار و افراد با سیستم ایمنی ضعیف در معرض خطر افزایش عوارض هستند. ویسکانسین تا کنون 431 مورد سرخک را در 13 شهرستان در سال جاری گزارش کرده است که نشان دهنده بالاترین تعداد موارد مشاهده شده در این ایالت در بیش از 35 سال است. در میان

Nocturne Episode 3, “Eyes on the Inside,” ended with a jaw-dropping reveal that answered one of the Apple TV show’s most crucial questions.

At the same time, the mysterious final scene likely left viewers confused and wondering what — and crucially, who — they just laid eyes on. So Decider spoke with EP and co-showrunner John Hlavin to get clarity.

Nocturne Episode 3 spoilers ahead.

For those who need a refresher, Episode 3 flashed back to show Sally Gifford (Kersti Bryan) and her family flee their home, while Jonah (Liev Schreiber) investigated her disappearance and a curious symbol carved into trees. Meanwhile, in Riverside Psychiatric Hospital, Saga (Zazie Beetz) went undercover as Esther, while Jurek (Stephen Graham) continued strengthening his relationship with Karl (Rory Culkin) in the RHU.

As the stakes grew higher and the clock ticked, “Eyes on the Inside” built up to an unexpected ending that kept characters in the dark but gave viewers some crucial insight. So who was in Nocturne Episode 3’s ending? What did Sally see outside of her house? Who is The Sandman? What’s Jurek doing in his cell? And what does that symbol mean?

Here’s what we know about Nocturne Episode 3, including quotes from Decider’s interview with Hlavin.

In the final minutes of Nocturne Episode 3, the task force gets an anonymous call from someone disguising their voice, warning, “STOP LOOKING FOR SALLY GIFFORD. SHE’S GONE. I TOOK HER. I TOOK THEM ALL. I’LL BURY THEM ALL. YOU’LL NEVER FIND THEM.” Nocturne then cuts to a person wearing a black hoodie, brown leather gloves, and a terrifying mask. They’re walking through what appears to be an underground tunnel with stone on both sides and water dripping. They push open a wooden door, then make their way to a sturdier metal door, remove the barricade that keeps it locked, and open it to reveal a terrified, emaciated girl sitting on a dirty mattress in an empty room. Nocturne shows us the view from the girl’s blurry eyes, and though we can’t see who’s in front of her, we do see a bit of the person’s mask in the light of a flashlight. We also hear heavy breathing, glass clinking, and the door creak closed behind them before the end credits roll. Horrifying.

So what the heck just happened? Who called the FBI with a warning? Who’s behind the mask? What are they doing to that girl? And is that young girl Felicia?! Let’s break Episode 3’s ending down with help from Hlavin.

First things first: Who’s the girl at the end of Nocturne Episode 3? Is that Felicia Frost? Is Felicia alive in Nocturne? Yes! Episode 3 takes place on “Felicia Search Day 4” and though Nocturne‘s writers could have kept the fact that Felicia (Abigail Donaghy) is still alive a mystery until much later in the season, Hlavin and the team felt it was important that viewers had the key piece of information early on, “in part because you have to understand why you’re watching the show, otherwise it becomes very intellectual.”

“We wanted to answer that question,” Hlavin told Decider over Zoom. “And it would have been a little bit almost preposterous that she would have already been gone, because then you wouldn’t have had the equality of smarts. Everyone has to be at the same place intellectually. And if one person has a giant piece of information that, ‘Oh, she’s already dead, and I’m using you guys,’ the audience reacts in a very different way. They kind of feel like, ‘Why are you so stupid? Don’t you know she’s gone?’ Keeping her alive keeps everybody at that same level of stakes. The stakes of, ‘Will you get her?’ But there are also emotional stakes.”

So who’s holding Felicia hostage? It’s not clear who called the authorities, or if they’re the same person we see in the mask, but as Jonah suspected, it’s unlikely that Jurek is slipping out of his cell to take care of business on the outside, so Nocturne leads us to believe that the person in the mask is Jurek’s accomplice, The Sandman.

As Michael recalled earlier in the episode, “Mom always said that The Sandman came in the night. That’s why you fell asleep.” When Jonah asked if the person who held Michael captive put him to sleep, Michael said, “It came in the room. His fingers were made of glass. You could hear them clacking.” He also confirmed he never saw The Sandman’s face, just heard his voice, because he was always wearing a mask and kept them in the dark. So, yeah! This is our guy.

Though the episode doesn’t explicitly reveal what’s making the clacking glass sound, in Episode 1, Nathan found an empty bottle of Sevoflurane by the mattress they found in their investigation. Sevoflurane is an anesthetic that Michael had in his blood and was found in every one of Jurek Walter’s victims, so we’re pretty sure The Sandman is using Sevoflurane to put his victims to sleep.

While we impatiently await more answers in Nocturne Episode 4, let’s run through a few other Episode 3 questions.

As Karl learns in Nocturne Episode 3, Sally Gifford had Karl’s job before he started in the RHU. She worked with Jurek, and now she’s missing. Though we don’t know what happened to Sally or where she and her family fled to, thanks to Jonah, we have reason to believe she’s still alive. After Jonah finds the Gifford family van off the side of the road, he notes he saw four sets of prints leaving the vehicle and no signs of struggle, which suggests they got out on foot. “I don’t think they were being pursued. I think she’s scared… she saw something or someone that spooked her.”

Though we didn’t see what was in Sally’s backyard before she panicked and fled her house with her family, both Jonah and Quinn assume she saw Jurek’s accomplice, aka The Sandman. So that’s the top theory at the moment!

Speaking of Jurek’s accomplice behind Sally’s house, Jonah also spends part of the episode investigating a cryptic symbol he found carved in trees in Sally’s backyard woods — the same symbol that was present at the burial sites of Cassie Ford and O’Leary and Cross. And essentially the same symbol Saga found herself staring at in Riverside. While the symbols may hold a deeper meaning, three episodes in, we only know as much as Jonah and the team, which is that they’re markers at crime scenes tied to Jurek Walter.

Speaking of Jurek, we once again see him stocking up on seemingly meaningless supplies in his cell. At the end of Episode 1, when he shoved what appeared to be a small black piece of tape in a secret hiding space under his sink/toilet, it wasn’t really clear what was going on. But in Episode 3, we see him save a plastic Jell-O cup from his meal, then use his shoe to scrape the petroleum jelly he conned Karl into slathering on his secretly self-inflicted back wounds into the Jell-O cup, then add it to his secret collection of stuff, which includes an assortment of random items, including a battery and wires. Uh oh! Looks like Jurek’s got a plan!

While you’re counting down the days until Nocturne‘s next episode, catch up on Decider’s interviews with Schreiber and Graham on how they prepped for their roles.

Stay tuned for more of DECIDER’s interview with Hlavin and the cast of Nocturne.

New episodes of Nocturne premiere Fridays on Apple TV.

DEAR ABBY: My husband and I have been happily married for 30 years. We both were previously widowed and have grown children and a large number of grandchildren. From the beginning of our marriage, we funded many things for our children — cars, college, weddings, eating out, shopping trips, vacations, etc. Because we’re now retired, we can no longer afford to foot the bill for everyone. Yet, since this pattern has gone on so long, it’s expected. No one even offers to pay for anything if they’re with us.

Because of this, we have decided to no longer participate in some family activities. We simply can’t pay for everything. None of the “kids” seems to realize that we’re trying to live within our adjusted means, or that even if we had the money, we should not be obligated to continually foot the bill.

On the other hand, on our special days (Father’s Day, Mother’s Day, birthdays, etc.) only one of the grown children even bothers to send us a card. At Christmas, all of them receive a nice card and a family check from us. The one who sends us the Christmas card includes a gift card. The other five seldom even respond with a “thank you.” Sadly, most of the grandchildren are the same way. Their birthday cards and checks are never acknowledged.

I’m ready to quit sending anything to anyone and act ignorant when a server brings the bill to our table filled with family. My husband feels these expenditures are like doling out their inheritance early. We both are by nature generous people, but I think we’ve been taken advantage of by those we love. Do you agree? — MONEY MAMA IN MICHIGAN

DEAR MAMA: Your children’s manners are atrocious, so it’s no wonder their laziness has been passed down to the next generation. However, some of the blame for this state of affairs lies with you and your husband, so I hate to accuse anyone of taking advantage of you.

At the time of your husband’s retirement, a family conference should have been held in which you explained your new financial reality to your children. Because that didn’t happen, they should not be blamed for assuming nothing has changed. Schedule that overdue conversation as soon as possible. When you do, feel free to mention how it makes you feel when your gifts are not acknowledged.

DEAR ABBY: Is it rude to tell a stranger or a customer that their zipper is down? I asked a few colleagues, and they all said they would want to be told. I did this twice with customers last week. Both appreciated it, and one said I was his “new best friend” for speaking up. What’s proper? Or should I “zip it”? — JUST TRYING TO HELP

DEAR TRYING: As long as the message is delivered subtly or privately, you are doing the person a favor. It falls into the category of telling someone there is toilet paper on their shoe, lipstick on their teeth or, perhaps, that they should wipe their nose again. It is a kindness.

Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.
news.content: بیشتر پوشش ما را در نتایج جستجوی خود مشاهده کنید. ابی عزیز: من و شوهرم 30 سال است که با هم ازدواج کرده ایم. ما هر دو قبلا بیوه بودیم و فرزندان بزرگ و تعداد زیادی نوه داریم. از ابتدای ازدواجمان، ما چیزهای زیادی را برای فرزندانمان تأمین می کردیم - ماشین، دانشگاه، عروسی، غذا خوردن، خرید، تعطیلات، و غیره. با این حال، از آنجایی که این الگو برای مدت طولانی ادامه داشته است، انتظار می رود. حتی اگر با ما باشد، هیچ کس پیشنهاد نمی کند برای چیزی پول بپردازد. به همین دلیل، ما تصمیم گرفته ایم دیگر در برخی از فعالیت های خانوادگی شرکت نکنیم. ما به سادگی نمی توانیم برای همه چیز هزینه کنیم. به نظر می‌رسد هیچ یک از «بچه‌ها» نمی‌دانند که ما سعی می‌کنیم با امکانات خود زندگی کنیم، یا حتی اگر پول داشته باشیم، نباید مجبور به پرداخت مداوم این صورت‌حساب باشیم. از طرف دیگر، در روزهای خاص ما (روز پدر، روز مادر، تولد و غیره) فقط یکی از بچه های بالغ حتی زحمت می کشد برای ما کارت بفرستد. در کریسمس، همه آنها یک کارت خوب و یک چک خانوادگی از ما دریافت می کنند. کسی که کارت کریسمس را برای ما ارسال می کند یک کارت هدیه نیز دارد. پنج نفر دیگر حتی به ندرت با "متشکرم" پاسخ می دهند. متاسفانه اکثر نوه ها همینطور هستند. کارت تولد و چک آنها هرگز تایید نمی شود. من حاضرم از ارسال هر چیزی برای هر کسی دست بکشم و وقتی سروری صورتحساب را پر از خانواده سر میز ما بیاورد، نادان عمل کنم. شوهرم احساس می‌کند این هزینه‌ها مانند خرج کردن خود هستند

news.originalContent:
His historic victory in Michigan shows that Muslim Americans need not abandon their identity or Palestine to succeed in politics.

Messages popped up on my WhatsApp account from New York, Gaza, Pakistan and Australia. Friends and colleagues were following Michigan’s Senate race, talking excitedly about Abdul El-Sayed. As the results from Wayne County sealed his victory on Tuesday, I felt something I had rarely felt before in American politics: not a muted relief that someone had lost but genuine joy and hope that someone had won.

El-Sayed, a physician and former Detroit health director, defeated Republican Mike Rogers. He will be the first Muslim ever elected to the United States Senate. As a Muslim American from Michigan, this hit home.

Like many in Michigan’s Muslim community, I knew of Abdul long before he became a fixture in national headlines, from his 2018 gubernatorial campaign to his Friday sermons in local mosques. As Ramadan began this year, I attended one of his town halls for Muslim constituents. Before a few dozen community members and leaders, Abdul pledged to fight for all Michiganders. His sincerity and commitment to that pledge remained evident even as the pressures of the campaign intensified. I have seen him attend funerals for community members near my home and watched him go from person to person, greeting people with kindness. Even in the final days of an exhausting campaign, he responded personally to messages from the community, including mine.

We attended the same university, the University of Michigan, where he once helped lead the Muslim Students’ Association. I later served as a college student body president there. Just days before the election, Muslim alumni (including me) invited him to a football tailgate party with students, parents and graduates. His former teachers and students have spoken to me with pride about the person they knew.

Muslim Americans are often asked to celebrate any politician who occasionally says “salaam” or appears in a mosque before Election Day. Abdul was not an outsider to our community coming to court us. He belonged to it.

During the campaign, I welcomed hundreds of local Muslim community members, out-of-state political candidates canvassing for him and members of his staff into my home. People heard from those closest to him what this race could mean for Muslim Americans. The enthusiasm felt different from the familiar, dispiriting bargain of voting mainly to stop someone worse.

Two years ago, I wrote about why I would vote against genocide in the 2024 presidential election. That decision was shaped by my work with Palestinian healthcare workers, by witnessing the realities in Palestine firsthand and by outrage at the Biden-Harris administration’s complicity in the genocide in Gaza. Neither I nor many of Michigan’s Muslims have forgotten. But this time, the ballot offered something other than just a protest vote: a candidate who had opposed Israel’s genocide against Palestinians from the outset while also caring about the range of issues affecting Michiganders.

His willingness to speak truth to power attracted immense hostility from Washington’s elites. President Donald Trump repeatedly mocked Abdul’s name, treating “Muhammad” – his middle name, meaning “the praised one” – as an insult. Political opponents and even some voters insinuated that his faith alone made him suspect, recycling unsubstantiated allegations tying him to groups and movements he did not belong to.

Abdul responded with dignity and directness. When critics made his name the issue, he spoke about groceries, housing, healthcare and affordability. When challenged over his opposition to genocide, he questioned the premise that wanting children to live free of bombs was somehow hateful. He did not accept the proposition that a Muslim must disown his community or Palestine to qualify for public office.

And most importantly, he fought back. Many Muslim voters I spoke to felt they had found someone willing to fight for them, to challenge the presumptions and racism of journalists, pundits and media outlets rather than accept their unjust framing.

His victory speech began with the words his opponents had tried to weaponise: “My name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed.” He recalled having said “inshallah” – “God willing” – whenever he was asked about winning. Now, he said, it was time for “alhamdulillah”, or “Praise be to God.”

That moment was electric, not because Arabic phrases alone are a sign of solidarity – even former President Joe Biden said “inshallah” in a debate before proceeding to commit genocide against Palestinians and aid the bombing of mosques and burning of Qurans – but because his Muslim identity had survived a countrywide effort by special interest groups and racists to make it disqualifying. His faith, Islam, is a value system he actively chooses every day, a commitment he strives to live out in public life. His being Muslim mattered to me more than his Arab ethnicity or ancestral origins, a simple happenstance of birth.

There was money behind the attempt to stop him too. The American Israel Public Affairs Committee’s (AIPAC’s) affiliated super PAC spent roughly $30m in Michigan’s Democratic primary, an extraordinary investment to defeat someone who openly opposed US support for Israel’s genocide and apartheid. In his victory speech, Abdul thanked AIPAC for the chance to beat it twice. One loss will not dissolve the lobbying group’s power. But Michigan demonstrated that AIPAC spending need not amount to a veto over who can win.

After Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s victory in New York, sceptics suggested that a Muslim candidate outspoken about Palestine could only win in a liberal metropolis, not a state that Trump carried in 2024. El-Sayed travelled from small towns and villages to industrial cities and suburbs, visiting churches and mosques, and he won statewide.

Michigan has long been a centre of Muslim American life, from Dearborn’s famous Arab restaurants and coffee houses to Hamtramck, the first Muslim-majority city in the US. Generations have built mosques, schools, businesses and institutions while enduring suspicion and discrimination. There is irony in Michigan electing a Muslim alumnus of the University of Michigan, which has faced legal challenges over its treatment of antigenocide protesters. Some of the voices that were treated as dangerous on campus found a home at the ballot box for the first time.

Other Muslims across the country made history too. My mentor, friend and colleague Adam Hamawy, with whom I served on a medical mission in Palestine documenting harm to people’s health, won his congressional race in New Jersey and travelled to Michigan to support Abdul. Darializa Avila Chevalier, Aber Kawas, Nabeela Syed and so many others won seats in Congress and state legislatures across the country, refusing to accept that their silence on human rights abuses is the price of participation.

Yet our celebration does not mean we have suspended all judgement. Some Muslims I spoke with vehemently opposed Abdul’s decision to campaign alongside former Vice President Kamala Harris and former President Barack Obama. Their administrations’ policies, from facilitating the genocide in Gaza to conducting drone strikes against civilians in multiple Muslim-majority countries, remain at the forefront of people’s minds. I understood their anger and shared their apprehensions about normalising the killers of children. Yet many of us still voted for Abdul because we believed in his sincerity and because he had repeatedly made clear that he did not agree with every policy of those backing his campaign. I am under no illusion that one senator alone will end the systems and structures of exploitation that fund war machines abroad and fail their own communities at home. Muslim representation risks becoming hollow if mistaken for the only tool for liberation.

And that is precisely why the substance of his campaign matters. Abdul connected the fight against endless war to the fight for healthcare, clean water and a liveable wage. He spoke of a mother trying to keep her children on lifesaving medication and a worker fighting for a union. He insisted that the money spent destroying someone else’s children has a cost for children in the US too. His politics asked whether Americans could both recognise their own self-interest and show humanity towards others.

His election does not make US government policies any more just overnight. It does not bring back a single Palestinian child. It does not absolve the Democrats, Washington or any of us of complicity. And it certainly does not entitle Abdul to six years in the Senate without scrutiny.

But it destroys one convenient lie: that Muslim Americans must choose between being unapologetically Muslim and belonging fully to American public life.

For years, we were told to lower our voices, soften our names and reconsider what we advocate for if we wanted to succeed. On Tuesday, Michigan delivered its verdict. The man they tried to make unelectable will now sit in the US Senate. Alhamdulillah, he does not need to become less Muslim to serve his state – and the rest of us do not need to police who we are to demand a better future for ourselves and the generations to come.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.
news.content: پیروزی تاریخی او در میشیگان نشان می‌دهد که آمریکایی‌های مسلمان برای موفقیت در سیاست نیازی به ترک هویت یا فلسطین خود ندارند. پیام‌هایی از نیویورک، غزه، پاکستان و استرالیا در حساب WhatsApp من ظاهر شد. دوستان و همکاران مسابقه سنای میشیگان را دنبال می کردند و با هیجان در مورد عبدالالسید صحبت می کردند. از آنجایی که نتایج وین کانتی در روز سه‌شنبه پیروزی او را امضا کرد، چیزی را احساس کردم که قبلاً به ندرت در سیاست آمریکا احساس می‌کردم: نه آرامشی که کسی از دست داده بود، بلکه شادی و امید واقعی بود که کسی پیروز شده بود. السید، پزشک و مدیر سابق بهداشت دیترویت، مایک راجرز جمهوری‌خواه را شکست داد. او اولین مسلمانی خواهد بود که در سنای ایالات متحده انتخاب می شود. به عنوان یک آمریکایی مسلمان اهل میشیگان، این موضوع به خانه رسید. مانند بسیاری از افراد جامعه مسلمان میشیگان، من مدت‌ها قبل از اینکه عبدالله یکی از مهره‌های اصلی خبرهای ملی شود، از مبارزات انتخاباتی فرمانداری سال 2018 تا خطبه‌های نماز جمعه در مساجد محلی، او را می‌شناختم. با شروع ماه رمضان امسال، من در یکی از تالارهای شهر او برای مسلمانان شرکت کردم. قبل از چند ده عضو و رهبران جامعه، عبدل متعهد شد که برای همه مردم میشیگاند مبارزه کند. صداقت و تعهد او به این عهد حتی با تشدید فشارهای مبارزات انتخاباتی مشهود بود. من او را دیده‌ام که در مراسم تشییع جنازه اعضای جامعه در نزدیکی خانه‌ام شرکت می‌کند و او را تماشا می‌کردم که از فردی به فرد دیگر می‌رفت و با مهربانی به مردم سلام می‌کرد. حتی در روزهای پایانی یک کمپین طاقت فرسا، او شخصا به پیام های جامعه از جمله پیام من پاسخ داد.

news.originalContent:
The US midterms were a rejection of Donald Trump’s politics of division, but his legacy may be impossible to undo.

“I think it’s safe to say that we are tired of being pitted against each other. We are tired of being told to hate each other. It has been 10 years of this kind of politics. Politics as blood sport. Politics as trolling and owning. Politics as professional wrestling. It tears families apart. It ends friendships, and it leaves us all feeling terrible all the time.”

So said Senator-elect James Talarico in his victory speech on election night after he won the first United States Senate seat in Texas for the Democratic Party in almost 40 years.

I don’t like Talarico or his policies, but I agree with him on one thing: The American people are tired of being pitted against one another. We need more uniters and fewer dividers in the Republican Party and US politics in general.

This is the conclusion many American voters seem to have reached after 10 years of Donald Trump dominating the right.

A decade ago, he forcefully entered the political scene with a radically different approach and provocative rhetoric. He won his first US presidential election by attacking his opponents with clever and cutting nicknames. Crooked Hillary. Low-energy Jeb. Pocahontas. Little Marco. Crazy Bernie. Lying Ted.

All were aimed at diminishing his rivals in ways that only a rapturous crowd of adoring MAGA fans could really appreciate. His attacks played well on social media and reflected an American culture that was far less deferential to the political establishment, far coarser in its language and far more interested in being entertained than being informed.

Trump’s attacks, performed live at his raucous rallies, had all the earmarks of a professional wrestling bout. It was blood sport at its most basic level. And Trump’s supporters ate it up, loving how he stood up to an elite that obviously despised them.

His opponent in the 2016 presidential election, Hillary Clinton, called half of his supporters a “basket of deplorables”.

Seven years before Trump formally entered the race for the White House, Barack Obama in a speech in San Francisco had said that people like them “get bitter, they cling to guns or religion or antipathy to people who aren’t like them or anti-immigrant sentiment or anti-trade sentiment as a way to explain their frustrations”.

Trump gathered up these angry voters, many of whom had protested during the Tea Party movement, and created “Make America Great Again” (MAGA). They loved the visceral way Trump communicated. They loved that he promised to end illegal immigration and free-trade policies that destroyed manufacturing jobs.

Trump’s rhetoric, coarse as it was, seemed honest, authentic, unscripted, and totally real, not poll-tested, not AI-generated, not written by expensive speechwriters. Trump was talking to them, not at them. He had listened to their fears and promised to fight back with a vengeance.

When Trump claimed the political establishment had stolen his re-election, he didn’t sit idly by, accepting the results. He consulted his lawyers, came up with a dubious legal strategy and then unleashed his supporters on Capitol Hill, hoping upon hope that their pressure would bend the hallowed traditions of presidential succession to his will. It didn’t work, but it also didn’t disqualify him.

Over the four years of President Joe Biden’s administration, Trump survived legal attacks, threats of imprisonment and assassination attempts to become an invincible force who seized power again in 2024. His ascent seemed like destiny.

But as it often does, the fickle winds of the electorate changed direction. They used to love his unconventional approach to politics, but now they wanted him to deliver on his promises to lower inflation and gas prices. He had once promised to keep us out of foreign wars, but that promise was broken, too. Perhaps he had a good reason to attack Iran, but he failed to make a convincing case to the American public, and voters quickly grew disenchanted with another broken promise. The vice president himself said that the war is what cost the Republicans the election. But it was more than just the war. Voters were tired of the whole act.

When Trump told his voters to imagine that he was on the ballot, it wasn’t just his supporters who made this election a referendum on Trump. So too did angry Democrats, disgusted independents and more than a few former MAGA minions.

They said this election was about affordability, but it really was about an undisciplined president who refused to colour inside the lines, who blundered into a costly war, who didn’t stop his administration from detaining and deporting high school baseball coaches and Uber drivers and domestic employees, and harboured too many white supremacists within his ranks.

He alienated women, Hispanics, Asians, Arabs, African Americans and offended well-educated Midwesterners who couldn’t stomach his language or his antics any longer. The great MAGA coalition that he assembled for his historic 2024 victory dissipated in one election night, tired of the nonsense and wanting a change in direction.

Things are so bad for Republicans that they lost all kinds of members, from House leaders like Richard Hudson, to tremendously flawed MAGA warriors like Ken Paxton to seasoned and effective Appropriators like Susan Collins. Conservative Republicans lost. Traditional Republicans lost. Moderate Republicans lost. All kinds of Republicans lost. It is a total and complete rejection of the GOP, top to bottom. An unmitigated disaster.

There are two questions that remain. What will happen to the MAGA movement now? And can we ever return to the good old days before Trump made politics a blood sport more akin to Ultimate Fighting than to the World Wrestling Federation?

The answer is this: Unless Republicans fundamentally change how they communicate to voters and what they promise to do for them, they will not win another election. MAGA will be lost forever. Governing is about building coalitions, not about belittling potential allies with sophomoric attacks and needlessly partisan rhetoric.

Like Andrew Jackson, President Trump has forever changed American politics, and it is highly unlikely that we will ever completely return to the good old days of disagreeing without being disagreeable. But voters showed that they had grown tired of Mr. Trump’s brand of disagreeableness by delivering to the Democrats a huge political victory.

This election was not an endorsement of Democratic policies. It was a referendum on Trumpism and his caustic brand of politics. We will see if he got the message.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

انتخابات میان‌دوره‌ای ایالات متحده رد سیاست تفرقه‌ای دونالد ترامپ بود، اما ممکن است لغو میراث او غیرممکن باشد. «من فکر می‌کنم به جرات می‌توان گفت که از قرار گرفتن در برابر یکدیگر خسته شده‌ایم. از اینکه به ما می‌گویند از یکدیگر متنفر باشید، خسته شده‌ایم. ۱۰ سال از این نوع سیاست می‌گذرد. سیاست به عنوان خون‌رسانی به خانواده‌ها. جدا این به دوستی ها پایان می دهد و باعث می شود همه ما همیشه احساس وحشتناکی داشته باشیم."
جیمز تالاریکو، سناتور منتخب، در سخنرانی پیروزی خود در شب انتخابات، پس از کسب اولین کرسی سنای ایالات متحده در تگزاس برای حزب دموکرات پس از تقریباً 40 سال، گفت. من تالاریکو یا سیاست های او را دوست ندارم، اما در یک چیز با او موافقم: مردم آمریکا از قرار گرفتن در برابر یکدیگر خسته شده اند. ما در حزب جمهوری خواه و سیاست ایالات متحده به طور کلی به متحدان بیشتر و تفرقه افکنان کمتری نیاز داریم. این نتیجه ای است که به نظر می رسد بسیاری از رأی دهندگان آمریکایی پس از 10 سال تسلط دونالد ترامپ بر جناح راست به این نتیجه رسیده اند. یک دهه پیش، او با رویکردی کاملاً متفاوت و لفاظی های تحریک آمیز با قدرت وارد صحنه سیاسی شد. او اولین انتخابات ریاست جمهوری آمریکا را با حمله به مخالفانش با نام مستعار زیرکانه و بریده برنده شد. هیلاری کج. جب کم انرژی پوکاهونتاس مارکو کوچولو برنی دیوانه هدف همه دروغگویان تد، کاهش دادن رقبای خود به شیوه‌هایی بود که فقط یک جمعیت خشمگین از طرفداران MAGA واقعاً می‌توانستند قدردانی کنند. حملات او در رسانه های اجتماعی خوب بازی کرد و منعکس شد

news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

Rosie O’Donnell dabbled in the idea of returning to the States while celebrating the midterm election results.

O’Donnell – a consistent critic of the current administration – fled the United States for Ireland after Donald Trump was elected president for a second term in 2024.

While the former talk show host relished life across the pond, she’s now thinking about moving back home to New York, and told The Washington Post that Dublin is “beautiful — we love it here, but my family’s not here.”

She added, “And I miss my grown kids. I miss my grandson that was born six months ago. And I feel like I’ve missed half his life already and don’t want to miss any more.”

The “A League of Their Own” star has four children with ex-wife Kelli Carpenter, and one child with late ex-wife Michelle Rounds.

O’Donnell chimed in on TikTok to praise the blue wave that hit the States following Tuesday’s midterms, where Democrats won control of the house, in addition to capturing the Senate majority.

“It’s a beautiful morning in the world,” she said. “The Trump regime is over, thank you America. I knew we would do it; I knew it in my heart.”

“You gotta believe people, and you did, and you showed up. And we gave a very loud and clear message to Trump … and his partners in cruelty. His criminal friends – Enough, we’ve had enough.”

O’Donnell noted that she “went to bed early” in Dublin while returns came back on election night in the States.

“I didn’t think I could stay up; I was so anxious,” she said. “I went to bed and at 3 o’clock in the morning – ding, ding, ding, ding – everyone started texting me and I started to cry.”

“I was so overwhelmed with emotion – overwhelmed – and I got up this morning and I took a shower and I put on my blue jumper … and I’m like, I’m wearing blue today.”

O’Donnell said she was “so proud of all of us, of our country” before reflecting on the “unconstitutional, un-American things that this administration has perpetrated on the people of this country and the world.”

“Let the investigations begin, really,” O’Donnell said. “This is a glorious day.”

The White House responded in a statement to Fox News Digital, saying, “Rosie O’Donnell is a nasty woman and a total slob whose brain has been completely destroyed by Trump Derangement Syndrome.”

Earlier this year, O’Donnell wrapped up guest-hosting fellow Trump critic Jimmy Kimmel’s late-night show, where she called the president “orange Voldemort.”

“I’ve really enjoyed my time here thanks to everyone who’s been watching this week, especially the hungry, hungry hypocrite in the White House,” she said during her final opening monologue.

“Most of all, I’d like to thank Jimmy Kimmel for inviting me to do this and for reminding everyone that we have the right to free speech in this country, whether orange Voldemort likes it or not.”

O’Donnell and the president have traded jabs for years, and Trump threatened to revoke the comedian’s citizenship after she fled to Ireland in 2025.

The decades-long feud stems back to 2006 after O’Donnell criticized him when she was a host on “The View” about his decision to be lenient toward a Miss USA winner who had been accused of drug use and other bad behavior.
news.content:
پوشش های بیشتری را در نتایج جستجوی خود مشاهده کنید. رزی اودانل در حالی که نتایج انتخابات میان دوره ای را جشن می گرفت، ایده بازگشت به ایالات متحده را مطرح کرد. اودانل - از منتقدان همیشگی دولت فعلی - پس از انتخاب دونالد ترامپ برای دومین دوره رئیس جمهور در سال 2024 از ایالات متحده به ایرلند گریخت. در حالی که مجری سابق برنامه گفتگو از زندگی آن سوی برکه لذت می برد، او اکنون به بازگشت به خانه به نیویورک فکر می کند و به واشنگتن پست گفت که دوبلین "زیبا است - ما اینجا را دوست داریم، اما خانواده من اینجا نیستند."
او افزود: "و من دلم برای بچه های بزرگم تنگ شده است. دلم برای نوه ام که شش ماه پیش به دنیا آمد، تنگ شده است. و احساس می کنم نیمی از زندگی او را از دست داده ام و دیگر نمی خواهم چیزی را از دست بدهم." ستاره «A League of their Own» دارای چهار فرزند با همسر سابق کلی کارپنتر و یک فرزند از همسر سابق سابق خود میشل راندز است. او دانل در TikTok شرکت کرد تا از موج آبی ای که پس از انتخابات میان دوره ای روز سه شنبه به ایالات متحده رسید، جایی که دموکرات ها کنترل مجلس را به دست آوردند، علاوه بر اینکه اکثریت مجلس سنا را به دست آوردند، ستایش کرد. رژیم ترامپ تمام شده است، متشکرم آمریکا. می دانستم که این کار را خواهیم کرد. من آن را در قلبم می دانستم.»
"شما باید مردم را باور کنید، و این کار را کردید و ظاهر شدید. و ما پیامی بسیار بلند و واضح به ترامپ و شرکای او در ظلم دادیم. دوستان جنایتکار او - بس است، بس است.»
اودانل خاطرنشان کرد که او "زود به رختخواب رفت" در دوبلین در حالی که در شب انتخابات در ایالات متحده بازگشت.

news.originalContent:
Judge Tanya Chutkan orders a 14-day pause on the so-called ‘Arc de Trump’ project in Washington, DC.

A United States federal judge has ordered a temporary block on the construction of President Donald Trump’s 250ft (76-metre) “triumphal arch” in Washington DC.

US District Judge Tanya Chutkan on Friday, ordered a 14-day pause on any construction on the arch, despite the Trump administration last week saying it could begin as soon as Thursday.

The National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC) held a nine-hour hearing on Thursday, which resulted in a final vote of 8-4 in approval of the arch, despite the protest of dozens of witnesses who were against the construction.

Judge Chutkan’s decision follows a series of lawsuits that have been filed challenging the construction of the arch, including a group of Vietnam war veterans, who filed a suit in February.

Trump has proposed building the arch by the Arlington National Cemetery, where war veterans are buried, which caused concerns that it could block the view between the cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial.

The veterans said in a court filing that the line of sight between the two was “carefully designed to symbolise the unification of the country after the Civil War and the strength of a united nation”.

Trump first proposed the arch last year to mark 250 years of US independence, claiming it would be like other famous arches, such as the Arc de Triomphe built in Paris in 1836.

The so-called “Arc de Trump” is only one of many projects Trump has proposed in Washington. On Friday, he signed a proclamation designating his Oval Office and Cabinet room as a national monument.

Many of his plans have been blocked in the past by several judges, and after the Democrats won control of Congress in the midterm elections this week, those plans could face increased scrutiny.
news.content: قاضی تانیا چوتکان دستور توقف 14 روزه پروژه موسوم به "طاق ترامپ" در واشنگتن دی سی را صادر کرد. یک قاضی فدرال ایالات متحده دستور توقف موقت ساخت طاق پیروزی 250 فوتی (76 متری) رئیس جمهور دونالد ترامپ در واشنگتن دی سی را صادر کرد. دولت ترامپ هفته گذشته اعلام کرد که می تواند از روز پنجشنبه آغاز شود. کمیسیون برنامه ریزی سرمایه ملی (NCPC) روز پنجشنبه یک جلسه استماع نه ساعته برگزار کرد که با وجود اعتراض ده ها شاهدی که مخالف ساخت و ساز بودند، رای نهایی با 8-4 رای به تصویب رسید. تصمیم قاضی چوتکان به دنبال مجموعه ای از شکایت هایی است که برای به چالش کشیدن ساخت طاق، از جمله یک گروه کهنه سرباز در جنگ ویتنام، شکایت کرده اند. ترامپ پیشنهاد کرده است که این طاق را در گورستان ملی آرلینگتون، جایی که جانبازان جنگ دفن می‌کنند، بسازد، که این نگرانی‌ها را به وجود آورد که می‌تواند دید بین گورستان و بنای یادبود لینکلن را مسدود کند. کهنه سربازان در پرونده دادگاه گفتند که خط دید بین این دو "با دقت طراحی شده است تا نماد اتحاد کشور پس از جنگ داخلی و قدرت ملت" باشد. ترامپ برای اولین بار سال گذشته این طاق را به مناسبت 250 سال استقلال ایالات متحده پیشنهاد کرد و ادعا کرد که این طاق مانند طاق های معروف دیگر مانند طاق پیروزی ساخته شده در پاریس در سال 1836 خواهد بود. به اصطلاح "طاق ترامپ" تنها یکی از بسیاری از طاق های معروف است.

news.originalContent:
Lebanon faces renewed fears of another Israeli escalation, with residents preparing for potential conflict in the south.

Beirut, Lebanon – During Israel’s intensification of its war on Lebanon in March, Aya stayed at her home in Abbasiyeh, in southern Lebanon, despite the risks. At one point, she says, her neighbour’s house was targeted by an Israeli attack.

The attacks have subsided after an ostensible ceasefire was initially announced in April. But the sounds of war have not ceased.

“There’s always drones around and sounds of detonations, but we’ve grown thick skin,” she told Al Jazeera.

In recent weeks, however, fears have intensified around a potential third Israeli intensification since 2024. Many Lebanese are now living in limbo, especially those in areas that previously witnessed intense Israeli attacks.

Aya said her family has prepared extra medication for her grandparents, in case a new round of conflict makes it difficult to obtain. Others are preparing bags and extra food, and keeping their electronic devices charged should the attacks start again.

She also said she would leave her home if Israeli attacks intensified again, rather than stay as she had before.

“I don’t have the energy for this anymore,” she said. Instead, she has been thinking about leaving Lebanon.

“I just can’t handle going through another displacement, especially while watching people around me carry on with their lives as if nothing is happening,” she said. “I know it’s normal, but for me it’s mentally exhausting.”

The Lebanese Shia group Hezbollah and Israel have been at war since October 2023. Since then, Israel has killed around 9,000 people in Lebanon, according to the Lebanese health ministry, mostly during escalations in the autumn of 2024 and in March and April 2026. Israel invaded Lebanon during each offensive and has since occupied up to 10 kilometres of territory, where it has established a so-called “Yellow Line”. Below that line, Israel continues to destroy towns and villages, while it has already made border areas uninhabitable, possibly for years to come.

A ceasefire was announced in April, just over a week after Israel launched more than 100 attacks on Lebanon in less than 10 minutes, killing more than 350 people. Then in June, Beirut and Tel Aviv signed a US-brokered framework agreement to set up “pilot zones”, as part of which the Israeli military would withdraw from those areas and the Lebanese army would move in to disarm Hezbollah.

Following the ceasefire and framework agreement, active fighting between Hezbollah and Israel has eased, despite Israel’s ongoing attacks and destruction of homes and infrastructure in the far south of Lebanon. Those who live above the Yellow Line are mostly out of the line of fire but hear constant explosions and drones, and at times have struggled to access their land.

In recent weeks, US President Donald Trump has reportedly considered launching another round of attacks on Iran, in coordination with Israel. Iran has warned that if such an attack happens, it would retaliate against targets in the region. This has led to questions over whether Hezbollah, which is backed by Iran, would return to conducting its own attacks against Israel.

Israeli officials have also accused the Lebanese army of failing to meet its part of the framework deal – something the Lebanese army denies – in what analysts say might be an effort to build justification for another bombing campaign in Lebanon.

“When it comes to Lebanon, Israel doesn’t need that instigation,” Mohamad Bazzi, a Lebanese political analyst, told Al Jazeera. “It destroyed more of the south under the ceasefire of April 17 than before it. Again and again, Israel has shown its willingness to carry out its policies, to destroy as much of south Lebanon as possible, to make it uninhabitable, and to punish the Shia community and there is no reason it won’t do more of the same if the US and Israel restart the Iran war on a large scale.”

In July 2024, Ramez, who did not want to use his real name for security reasons, was sitting in his bedroom in Beirut’s southern suburb of Haret Hreik when he heard loud explosions. Soon after, the neighbouring building collapsed on his apartment.

Since then, he has stayed in his family’s second home, about a half-hour drive southeast of Beirut.

“The war for me never really stopped,” he told Al Jazeera. “Going to sleep is a gamble between insomnia, nightmares or panic attacks. Even if every country in the world disposed of every single bomb and every single bullet and every single gun, the trauma will stay there.”

He said his family has postponed returning to his home in Beirut’s southern suburbs, known as Dahiyeh, over concerns the attacks could restart. “Personally, I can’t possibly even consider sleeping there without hallucinating the building collapsing in on me again.”

Ramez said he is keeping his batteries and power banks charged, his water supply steady for months and his car’s petrol tank full.

Other people interviewed by Al Jazeera who are from Dahiyeh or the south said they keep go-bags packed.

“People have been planning for a few months,” Karim Safieddine, a non-resident fellow with the Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy, told Al Jazeera. “Dahiyeh hasn’t been filled with people in the past few months. At night, it always empties a bit and everyone has a very, very delicate escape route that’s very quick.”

While general anxiety has gripped many in Lebanon over another round of intense fighting, people are also feeling the economic crunch.

The World Bank said in August that it expects inflation in Lebanon to rise to 17.5 percent this year.

And analysts fear that could have severe security consequences.

“As this cycle repeats itself, people get worn down, exhaust their savings and their goodwill, and I think that adds to the possibility of social explosion,” Bazzi said. “Lebanese society will blame Hezbollah for instigating against Israel and by extension [some will blame] the entire Shia community.”

Jad Dilati, a Lebanese analyst from Nabatieh, in southern Lebanon, said that some families have continued to pay rent for apartments in other parts of Lebanon in order “to secure alternative accommodation in case another war breaks out”.

But after three years of war, he said, “that’s a privilege that not everyone can afford”.

Analysts also warned that another round of fighting could increase sectarian tensions in the country. They say Israel has tried to foment internal strife in Lebanon, often by warning non-Shia communities in the south against hosting displaced people. And with people already barely getting by economically, another round of fighting could cause a sectarian spark.

“It is a combustible mix that could explode through something unexpected,” Bazzi said.

news.originalContent:
Israeli restrictions on teachers and pressure to adopt Israeli curriculum threaten Palestinian education in the city.

Jamal Shalabi is a 66-year-old chemistry teacher living in el-Bireh, in the occupied West Bank, but since 1998 he has taught in occupied East Jerusalem, making the commute through Israeli checkpoints every day.

The process was tiring, but it allowed him to work. But he now fears that soon won’t be the case, after he was informed by his school’s administration that he was one of 180 Palestinian teachers whose travel permits allowing them entry into East Jerusalem would be revoked upon their expiry at the end of the 2026-27 academic year.

The denial of entry permits to teachers is one of the most prominent restrictions imposed by Israel on schools in East Jerusalem, which, like the West Bank, is illegally occupied Palestinian territory, but which Israel considers part of a unified Jerusalem under its control.

Permits were already a problem for teachers like Shalabi this year, when the issuance of documents was delayed until September 15, two weeks after the academic year began. Permits were also delayed last January. The delays in both January and September led to school strikes in East Jerusalem, a move intended to exert pressure and demonstrate a unified stance against these Israeli measures.

Shalabi explained that even when the permits are approved, they are severely restrictive. The documents can only be used during specific hours, which teachers are not permitted to exceed. The teachers are also prohibited from being anywhere other than the schools.

“These permit restrictions have been in place since the war on Gaza in 2023; we can no longer reach the Al-Aqsa Mosque to pray, nor can we accompany students on school field trips, as the permits are strictly limited to the workplace,” he explained.

“Moreover, for the first time, we were barred from entering Jerusalem for an entire week during the recent Jewish holiday of Sukkot,” he added.

The permit restrictions come alongside wider measures affecting Palestinian education in East Jerusalem, including policies introduced under a plan approved by the Israeli government supposedly aimed at “reducing socioeconomic gaps” in East Jerusalem, whose population is majority Palestinian, despite Israeli efforts to increase the number of Jewish settlers.

The government plan also aims to increase the number of Palestinian students studying the Israeli curriculum. It does so by conditioning funding for new schools on the adoption of the Israeli curriculum, alongside programmes to train teachers within the Israeli education system.

A report by the Israeli human rights organisation Ir Amim warned that the policies exploit educational needs to undermine the autonomy of Palestinian education, as well as its national and cultural identity.

The report further warns of the repercussions of a law that prohibits the employment of teachers who hold university degrees from Palestinian educational institutions, a measure likely to exacerbate the existing shortage of teachers in East Jerusalem’s schools.

According to Ir Amim, approximately half of the education budget allocated under the Israeli government’s plan for East Jerusalem is directed towards expanding the teaching of the Israeli curriculum.

Furthermore, Israeli authorities make the adoption of this curriculum a prerequisite for the opening of new state-funded schools, which the organisation views as a form of pressure on both schools and parents to abandon the Palestinian curriculum.

The number of Palestinian students in East Jerusalem studying the Israeli curriculum was only in the hundreds 15 years ago. But by 2020, the figure had risen to more than 10,000.

The numbers have risen sharply since then. By 2024, it had risen to almost 20,000, according to Palestinian officials, and then to more than 27,000 the following year, according to figures cited by Ir Amim. Palestinian officials estimate that more than 45,000 students – approximately 38 percent of the total student population in the city – are now studying the Israeli curriculum in the 2026-27 academic year.

A principal of a school in East Jerusalem, who requested anonymity for fear of repercussions from Israeli authorities, told Al Jazeera that the expansion of the Israeli curriculum to tens of thousands of Palestinian students is the culmination of years of policies aimed at controlling education in East Jerusalem.

He argued that the situation represents an unprecedented threat to Palestinian education; the imposition of the Israeli curriculum is not merely an academic choice, but a policy designed to forcibly impose a new reality.

“This policy is not limited to official schools affiliated with the Israeli municipality; it also extends to private and community-based schools,” he added. “It involves [an attempt to replace the Palestinian curriculum] with a distorted version printed under the supervision of the municipality that erases and falsifies Palestinian history, geography, and national identity.”

The principal further explained that schools face direct threats, including the loss of funding, financial support, and operating licences if they refuse to introduce classes teaching the Israeli curriculum. This, he explained, was part of an Israeli five-year plan aimed at promoting the “Israelisation” of Palestinian education.

This included strict, rigorous oversight mechanisms, including on-site inspections and monitoring within classrooms, as well as the searching of students’ schoolbags to confiscate original Palestinian textbooks and prevent them from being taught.

“Israeli authorities intervene directly in the appointment of school principals and teachers, revoking the licences of those who don’t comply with their directives. Furthermore, this oversight extends to academic and personal persecution through targeting students, even for their personal social media posts or opinions, and employing disciplinary committees and police summonses to intimidate both staff and students,” the principal explained.

Al Jazeera has reached out to Israeli authorities, but has yet to receive a response.

Schools in East Jerusalem face a deficit of 2,283 classrooms, according to calculations by Ir Amim.

The organisation’s report warns that even if the Jerusalem Municipality’s plans to construct new classrooms are fully implemented, the crisis will not be resolved; a shortfall of approximately 1,100 classrooms is projected to persist by 2032.

For its part, the municipality estimates the current shortage at about 1,500 classrooms, a figure Ir Amim disputes because it says the calculation relies on outdated data.

Ramadan Awad, spokesperson for the Union of Parents’ Committees for Jerusalem Schools, told Al Jazeera that some classrooms contain as many as 42 students.

He explained that the shortage of classrooms is not merely a matter of insufficient space to enrol students; it also creates challenges within the schools themselves. Some institutions are forced to accommodate large numbers of students in cramped rooms, making it difficult for teachers to engage with individual students or monitor their academic progress.

Awad added that some schools have begun seeking out any available building to rent and convert into a school, even if it was originally a residential apartment or a commercial property.

“Such spaces often lack the essential features of a proper school, such as open courtyards, laboratories and rooms dedicated to extracurricular activities,” he said.
news.content: محدودیت‌های اسرائیل بر معلمان و فشار برای پذیرش برنامه درسی اسرائیل، آموزش فلسطین را در این شهر تهدید می‌کند. جمال شلبی یک معلم شیمی 66 ساله است که در البیره، در کرانه باختری اشغالی زندگی می‌کند، اما از سال 1998 او در اورشلیم شرقی اشغالی تدریس می‌کرد و هر روز به او اجازه رفت و آمد به اسرائیل را می‌داد. کار کردن اما او اکنون می ترسد که به زودی چنین نشود، زیرا از سوی مدیریت مدرسه اش به او اطلاع داده شد که یکی از 180 معلم فلسطینی است که مجوز سفر آنها که به آنها اجازه ورود به بیت المقدس شرقی را می دهد، در پایان سال تحصیلی 2026-2027 لغو می شود. ممانعت از ورود معلمان یکی از برجسته‌ترین محدودیت‌هایی است که اسرائیل برای مدارس در اورشلیم شرقی اعمال می‌کند، جایی که مانند کرانه باختری، سرزمین فلسطین اشغالی غیرقانونی است، اما اسرائیل آن را بخشی از بیت‌المقدس یکپارچه تحت کنترل خود می‌داند. مجوزها پیش از این دو هفته برای معلمانی مانند شالبی‌سو و اسناد دانشگاهی سال 15، یعنی زمانی که 15 سپتامبر لغو شد، مشکل ساز بود. آغاز شد. مجوزها نیز در ژانویه گذشته به تعویق افتاد. تأخیر در ژانویه و سپتامبر منجر به اعتصاب مدارس در اورشلیم شرقی شد، اقدامی که با هدف اعمال فشار و نشان دادن موضع واحد در برابر این اقدامات اسرائیل انجام شد. شلبی توضیح داد که حتی زمانی که مجوزها تأیید می شوند، به شدت محدود کننده هستند. مدارک فقط در ساعات مشخصی قابل استفاده است که معلمان آن را ندارند

news.originalContent:
Scandal is driving divisions between President Prabowo Subianto and predecessor Joko Widodo, sparking security concerns.

Indonesian police have named a fourth suspect in a scandal focused on the alleged wiretapping of President Prabowo Subianto.

At a news conference late on Thursday, police named a senior law enforcement official with the initials SU as the latest suspect. Three officials were arrested earlier in the week, in a scandal that has exposed a deepening rift between the president and his predecessor – and former ally – Joko Widodo, and sparked security concerns.

Police said that the new suspect served as monitoring chief at Indonesia’s Criminal Investigation Agency between 2010 and 2019. Local media later identified him as Slamet Uliandi.

Investigators alleged that SU, who was the head of the investigation agency’s information and technology unit from 2021 to 2026, gave the go-ahead for the wiretapping.

Cybercrime unit director Suhermanto told a media conference, “When the other two suspects were about to wiretap, they got approval from SU. They also asked his approval before deleting interception records.” Suhermanto added that SU had not yet been detained due to a health condition.

Three senior police officers were arrested on Tuesday, including the former national police chief and Prabowo’s chief of staff, Listyo Sigit Prabowo, who is widely known as a Widodo loyalist.

The case has piled more pressure on Prabowo, with public discontent growing over his costly populist policies and weakening investor confidence in Indonesia’s $1.5 trillion economy.

Police are still investigating the motives behind the attempts to intercept Prabowo’s communications, and have so far questioned 13 police officers and five criminal and IT experts.

The national police chief has also formed a special team to investigate the case, spokesperson Trunoyudo Wisnu Andiko said.

Jakarta remained calm on Thursday and Friday despite the deployment of thousands of troops in the wake of the wiretapping revelations. Military tents and buses were seen in the capital, as well as a small number of soldiers.

Prabowo took office in 2024 after winning the election in a landslide as the continuity candidate for Widodo. Joko Widodo’s son, Gibran Rakabuming Raka, was also elected as Prabowo’s vice president.

Lawmakers are now also considering a probe into the eligibility of Raka in what could be the first step towards removing him from office.
news.content: رسوایی باعث ایجاد اختلاف بین رئیس جمهور پرابوو سوبیانتو و جوکو ویدودو رئیس جمهور قبلی شده است و نگرانی های امنیتی را برانگیخته است. پلیس اندونزی مظنون چهارم را در یک رسوایی متمرکز بر شنود ادعایی رئیس جمهور پرابوو سوبیانتو معرفی کرده است. در یک کنفرانس خبری اواخر روز پنجشنبه، پلیس یک مقام ارشد اجرای قانون را به عنوان آخرین مظنون به نام SU معرفی کرد. سه مقام در اوایل هفته دستگیر شدند، در رسوایی که شکاف عمیق بین رئیس جمهور و سلف او - و متحد سابق - جوکو ویدودو را برملا کرد و نگرانی های امنیتی را برانگیخت. پلیس گفت که مظنون جدید بین سال های 2010 تا 2019 به عنوان رئیس نظارت در آژانس تحقیقات جنایی اندونزی خدمت کرده است. بازرسان ادعا کردند که SU که از سال 2021 تا 2026 رئیس واحد اطلاعات و فناوری آژانس تحقیقات بود، مجوز شنود را داده است. مدیر واحد جرایم سایبری، سوهرمانتو در یک کنفرانس رسانه ای گفت: "زمانی که دو مظنون دیگر در شرف استراق سمع بودند، از SU تاییدیه گرفتند. آنها همچنین قبل از حذف، سوابق شنود را تایید کردند. سوهرمانتو افزود که SU به دلیل وضعیت سلامتی هنوز بازداشت نشده است. سه افسر ارشد پلیس روز سه شنبه دستگیر شدند، از جمله رئیس پلیس ملی سابق و رئیس ستاد پرابوفو، لیستیو سیگیت پرابوو، که به طور گسترده به عنوان یک وفادار به ویدودو شناخته می شود. این پرونده فشار بیشتری را بر پرابوو وارد کرده است، با افزایش نارضایتی های عمومی او.

news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

A convicted child molester and illegal alien from Venezuela could soon be back on the streets unless authorities in Seattle ditch their sanctuary city policies and cooperate with federal immigration enforcement.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has sent a detainer request to the liberal Pacific Northwest enclave for Leomar Alexander Lopez Zambrano, asking that he be turned over rather than be released back into the US after his prison sentence concludes.

The clash between DHS and Seattle exacerbates longstanding tensions between President Donald Trump’s immigration officials and leaders in so-called sanctuary cities, which have thrown up roadblocks to law enforcement cooperating with federal enforcement authorities.

Going a step further, the outcome of Tuesday’s elections are putting even more of a microscope on the agency at the center of much controversy during Trump’s second term and is raising questions about which administration officials could face the wrath of a brand-new blue Congress.

“Sanctuary politicians in Washington are refusing to honor the ICE detainer and hand this disgusting criminal over to us after he finishes his prison sentence,” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement.

“This illegal alien has been convicted on TWO counts of child molestation.”

After the 2026 midterms, the matter in Seattle raises new questions of whether sanctuary cities will feel emboldened to double down on their efforts to block Trump’s agenda as Democrats prepare to retake a majority in the US Senate and House of Representatives.

To those like Hans von Spakovsky, an immigration expert with Advancing American Freedom (AAF), the political tide turning in Washington, DC, might encourage Democrat-run cities to go even further in stonewalling immigration enforcement agencies and making it harder for officials to do their jobs.

“I have no doubt that sanctuary jurisdictions will feel emboldened,” Spakovsky told Fox News Digital in the days after the Republican bloodbath.

“I also would not put it past [Democrats] to try to impeach Tom Homan for imagined wrongs because he has been the most effective czar of immigration enforcement of any administration in the past 50 years,” he said.

“I don’t think they would be successful, but, again, that will embolden defiance of federal immigration enforcement in sanctuary jurisdictions.”

In many cases, sanctuary cities simply cut off communication with federal law enforcement, and DHS fears that will be the case with Zambrano, the convicted Venezuelan child molester.

Zambrano is now approaching the end of a 15-month sentence, the point at which he would normally face deportation. But Mullin noted DHS would have no way of knowing when he was out of jail without Seattle’s cooperation.

“Sanctuary politicians care so much about illegal aliens that they’d rather release a convicted child molester than cooperate with federal law enforcement,” Mullin said.

When asked about Seattle’s cooperation with DHS, the agency responded by similarly emphasizing local-federal partnership.

“The safest way to arrest and remove criminal illegal aliens from our streets is by lodging arrest detainers. Because some sanctuary jurisdictions refuse to work with ICE law enforcement, criminal illegal aliens are released from jails into American communities to perpetuate more crimes. Seven of the top 10 safest cities in the United States cooperate with ICE,” the agency said in a statement.

In the wake of the election, some Republican onlookers believe similar concerns could emerge in other states, even red states like Texas.

Dan Bongino, a conservative commentator and podcast host, noted that the Lone Star State’s newly elected Democratic governor, Gina Hinojosa, voted against sanctuary city restrictions as a state legislator in 2017.

“Folks, Texas shares a border with Mexico. Do we need to ChatGPT this for people?” Bongino said in a recent podcast. “The only message [voters] are sending is you want your state to become a sanctuary, sitting on the border with Mexico for illegals who come into the United States.”

Spakovsky believes local resistance to immigration enforcement could coincide with congressional Democrats’ legislative efforts. He believes Democrats will attempt to target immigration enforcement resources through the congressional appropriations process, although he cast doubt on their effectiveness.

“Democrats will, no doubt, try to stop DHS from immigration enforcement and DOJ from prosecutions in the immigration area by trying to use the appropriations process to defund such enforcement at both agencies,” Spakovsky said.

“I am not sure they will be successful … especially if they tie such punitive measures with must-pass government funding that the president signs.”

Asked about whether DHS was concerned about an emboldened stance from sanctuary cities as Democrats retake control in the nation’s capital, DHS passed a statement along from Mullin.

“Deportations will continue,” the DHS chief said.

Officials from Seattle did not respond to requests for comment from Fox News Digital about Zambrano’s status.
news.content:
پوشش های بیشتری را در نتایج جستجوی خود مشاهده کنید. یک کودک آزاری محکوم و یک بیگانه غیرقانونی از ونزوئلا به زودی می تواند به خیابان ها بازگردد، مگر اینکه مقامات سیاتل از سیاست های شهر پناهگاه خود صرف نظر کنند و با مجریان مهاجرت فدرال همکاری کنند. اداره مهاجرت و گمرک (ICE) درخواست بازداشتی را برای لئومار الکساندر لوپز زامبرانو به منطقه لیبرال شمال غربی اقیانوس آرام ارسال کرده است و از او خواسته است که پس از پایان دوره محکومیتش به ایالات متحده بازگردانده شود. درگیری بین DHS و سیاتل تنش‌های طولانی‌مدت بین مقامات مهاجرت رئیس‌جمهور دونالد ترامپ و رهبران در شهرهای به اصطلاح پناهگاه را تشدید می‌کند، که موانعی را بر سر راه مجریان قانون که با مقامات اجرایی فدرال همکاری می‌کنند، ایجاد کرده است. یک گام جلوتر، نتیجه انتخابات روز سه‌شنبه، میکروسکوپ بیشتری را در مورد آژانس در مرکز جنجال‌های زیادی در دوره دوم ریاست‌جمهوری ترامپ قرار می‌دهد و این سوال را مطرح می‌کند که کدام مقامات دولت ممکن است با خشم یک کنگره کاملاً جدید آبی مواجه شوند. مارکوین مولین، وزیر امنیت داخلی در بیانیه‌ای گفت: «سیاستمداران پناهگاه در واشنگتن از احترام به بازداشت‌کننده ICE و تحویل این جنایتکار نفرت‌انگیز پس از پایان دوران زندان خودداری می‌کنند.» این بیگانه غیرقانونی به دو اتهام کودک آزاری محکوم شده است.
پس از انتخابات میان‌دوره‌ای 2026، موضوع در سیاتل پرسش‌های جدیدی را مطرح می‌کند که آیا شهرهای پناهگاهی احساس جسارت خواهند کرد یا خیر.

news.originalContent:
Announcement comes after majority of Israeli lawmakers endorse Eisenkot over Netanyahu.

Israel’s President Isaac Herzog has said he will name a candidate to form the country’s next government by Sunday, after a majority of lawmakers backed opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot over Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Herzog made the announcement on Thursday after holding marathon talks with parties elected to the 120-seat parliament, known as the Knesset.

Some 67 lawmakers endorsed Eisenkot, a former military chief, while 46 backed Netanyahu.

In televised remarks at the end of the talks, Herzog said that although the “results of the consultations may appear clear”, there were “mutual vetoes between the blocs and within the blocs themselves” that make it difficult to say who has the best chance of assembling a governing coalition.

He said he would hold “personal talks with some of the party leaders” over the Israeli weekend, which runs Friday-Saturday, and make a pick on Sunday.

Israel’s October 27 election left neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot with a clear path to a parliamentary majority, handing Herzog the difficult task of choosing a candidate in a deeply divided country.

Netanyahu’s Likud won the most seats of any single party with 27 in the 120-seat Knesset, ⁠but his wider religious-nationalist coalition garnered only 53 in total.

Eisenkot’s alliance of four Jewish-led parties, which spans the political spectrum from centre-left to right, won 48 seats despite polls that had predicted a close race.

Two parties representing Israel’s Palestinian minority won an unprecedented 19 seats.

Eisenkot, like Netanyahu, has ruled out forming a government with the Arab-led parties. Both of those parties nonetheless recommended him, giving him the support of a comfortable majority of lawmakers.

“We want to do things that we did not do in the past in order to remove this criminal government,” Ahmad Tibi, a senior member of the Joint List, which represents an alliance of Arab parties, told The Associated Press news agency.

Eisenkot’s party, Yashar, said his 67 recommendations were the most any candidate had received since 2015, and urged Herzog to give him the mandate “as soon as possible” so he could form a national emergency government.

Separately, Netanyahu suffered a setback on Thursday when United Torah Judaism, one of the two main ultra-Orthodox parties and a longtime ally, declined to recommend any candidate.

The party broke with Netanyahu over his coalition’s failure to pass legislation exempting ultra-Orthodox men from military service, The Times of Israel reported.

Yariv Oppenheimer, a member of the Democrats, a party in Eisenkot’s alliance, told Al Jazeera that he saw “no reason” Herzog would not choose Eisenkot on Sunday.

He said United Torah Judaism had signalled that its support was available for the right price, meaning that a good enough offer from Eisenkot could give him the numbers he needed.

“It’s very clear that Netanyahu doesn’t have a chance to establish a government at all,” he added.

Once nominated by Herzog, the candidate will have 28 days to try to forge a government, with a possible 14-day extension.

Netanyahu will remain prime minister in a caretaker government until a new coalition is formed, or through another election that must be held if no ⁠candidate succeeds.

Netanyahu, at risk of losing power, has seized on an investigation by election officials into possible vote tampering to cast doubt on the results, accusing Arab-led parties of stealing the vote.

Critics accuse Netanyahu and his partners of trying to undermine the results, which he denies.

Israel’s Central Election Committee said on ‌Wednesday that the election’s integrity had not been compromised. The head of the committee, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, has called on Israel’s elected officials to protect public trust rather than shake it.

“This is a real danger. One of the foundations of democracy is the peaceful transfer of power,” Sohlberg ‌told ‌Herzog at his residence on Wednesday. High voter turnout, including among the Arab minority, was a blessing, he said.

Netanyahu’s allies on the far-right, including National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, have called for the immediate arrest and interrogation of Arab party leaders.
news.content: این اعلامیه پس از حمایت اکثریت قانونگذاران اسرائیلی از آیزنکوت بر سر نتانیاهو صورت گرفت. آیزاک هرتزوگ، رئیس جمهور اسرائیل، پس از حمایت اکثریت قانونگذاران از گادی آیزنکوت، رهبر مخالفان بر سر بنیامین نتانیاهو، رئیس جمهور اسرائیل، گفت که نامزدی را برای تشکیل دولت بعدی کشور تا روز یکشنبه معرفی خواهد کرد. معروف به کنست حدود 67 قانونگذار از آیزنکوت، یک فرمانده سابق ارتش حمایت کردند، در حالی که 46 قانونگذار از نتانیاهو حمایت کردند. هرتزوگ در اظهارات تلویزیونی در پایان مذاکرات گفت که اگرچه "نتایج رایزنی ها ممکن است واضح به نظر برسد"، "وتوهای متقابلی بین بلوک ها و خود بلوک ها" وجود دارد که گفتن اینکه چه کسی بیشترین شانس را برای تشکیل یک دولت دارد دشوار است. او گفت که در آخر هفته اسرائیل، که از جمعه تا شنبه برگزار می‌شود، «مذاکرات شخصی با برخی از رهبران حزب» خواهد داشت و روز یکشنبه انتخاب خواهد کرد. انتخابات اسرائیل در 27 اکتبر نه نتانیاهو و نه آیزنکوت را در مسیر روشنی برای رسیدن به اکثریت پارلمانی باقی نگذاشت و وظیفه دشوار انتخاب نامزد در یک کشور عمیقاً تقسیم‌شده را به هرتزوگ واگذار کرد. حزب لیکود نتانیاهو با 27 کرسی در کنست 120 کرسی بیشترین کرسی ها را در میان هر حزبی به دست آورد، اما ائتلاف مذهبی-ملی گرای گسترده تر او در مجموع تنها 53 کرسی به دست آورد. اتحاد آیزنکوت متشکل از چهار حزب به رهبری یهودیان، که طیف سیاسی از چپ میانه تا 48 را در بر می گیرد.

See more of our coverage in your search results.

A Colorado police officer was killed and three more officers were wounded in a shooting Thursday evening near a bus outside Denver, authorities said.

Lakewood police said officers responded to a report of a suspicious person near the intersection of Colfax Avenue and Wadsworth Boulevard around 6:30 p.m., where they encountered a suspect attempting to board a bus.

The suspect opened fire on officers, striking four of them, Lakewood Police Public Information Officer John Romero said during a news conference.

“We are very sorry to report that one of those agents has been pronounced dead of their injuries,” Romero said.

The suspect was shot by police and pronounced dead at the scene, Romero said.

A civilian was also injured and transported to a local hospital.

Police did not immediately provide details about the extent of the injuries or the conditions of the three surviving officers.

Authorities said the suspect was attempting to board a Regional Transportation District (RTD) bus when officers approached.

“Within seconds of agents approaching the suspect, the suspect opened fire on our agents,” Romero said.

Romero also delivered an emotional message to the fallen officer’s family:

“We just want the family to know that we love them, that we’re here for them, and Lakewood Police Department is a family, and we will be here for each other.”

Colorado Gov. Jared Polis released a statement following the deadly shooting.

“Law enforcement put their lives on the line for our safety everyday and I am heartbroken to learn that a Lakewood Police Agent was killed in the line of duty this evening,” Polis wrote.

“My heart goes out to their family and friends,” he continued. “My thoughts are also with the three agents who are still receiving care at area hospitals, as well as the civilian who was wounded, and I wish them a full and speedy recovery. Thank you to law enforcement who run into danger to keep us safe and to protect our communities.”

Polis said the Colorado State Patrol was assisting at the scene and participating in a procession from the hospital honoring the fallen officer.

The Jefferson County Critical Incident Response Team is leading the investigation into the officer-involved shooting, with support from the Colorado Bureau of Investigation.

RTD also released a statement saying it was “deeply concerned” by the shooting.

“Our thoughts are with those affected directly by this incident,” the statement read. “The safety and well-being of our customers, employees, and partners remain our highest priority.”
news.content:
گزارش های بیشتر ما را در نتایج جستجوی خود مشاهده کنید. به گفته مقامات، یک افسر پلیس کلرادو در تیراندازی عصر پنجشنبه در نزدیکی اتوبوسی در خارج از دنور کشته و سه افسر دیگر زخمی شدند. پلیس لیک وود گفت که افسران به گزارش یک فرد مشکوک در نزدیکی تقاطع خیابان کولفکس و بلوار وادسورث حوالی ساعت 6:30 بعد از ظهر در حال تلاش برای سوار شدن به اتوبوسی بودند. جان رومرو افسر اطلاعات عمومی پلیس لیک وود طی یک کنفرانس خبری گفت که مظنون به سمت افسران تیراندازی کرد و چهار نفر از آنها را مورد ضرب و شتم قرار داد. رومرو گفت: "ما بسیار متأسفیم که گزارش می دهیم که یکی از این ماموران بر اثر جراحات جان خود را از دست داده است." رومرو گفت که مظنون مورد اصابت گلوله پلیس قرار گرفت و در صحنه مرگ اعلام شد. پلیس بلافاصله جزئیاتی در مورد میزان جراحات یا وضعیت سه افسر زنده‌مانده ارائه نکرد. مقامات گفتند که مظنون در حال تلاش برای سوار شدن به اتوبوس منطقه حمل‌ونقل منطقه‌ای (RTD) بود که افسران نزدیک شدند. رومرو گفت: «در عرض چند ثانیه که ماموران به مظنون نزدیک شدند، مظنون به سمت ماموران ما تیراندازی کرد. ما فقط می خواهیم خانواده بدانند که ما آنها را دوست داریم، که برای آنها اینجا هستیم، و اداره پلیس لیک وود یک خانواده است و ما برای یکدیگر اینجا خواهیم بود."
جارد پولیس فرماندار کلرادو پس از تیراندازی مرگبار بیانیه ای را منتشر کرد
